title: The North Woods
sceneText:
The disputed ground lies below the north slope, and getting there means going through a stretch with no path.

The stumps are new.

The cut faces are still pale and the chips at the edges have not gone black. Three weeks at the outside. You count them: eleven. And they are on your side of it, if the words “the stream to be the boundary” are read against the way the stream runs now.

variants.surveyed:
There were no stumps here the last time you walked this wood.

You remember how this stretch looked. That time you went further down along the slope, and looking back this piece of it was unbroken.

So these eleven came down after you took the post.

You have no way of judging whether it is over the line, but you can be certain when it happened.
variants.road:
A skid road runs through between the stumps, two deep ruts pressed into the ground, heading north.

You follow the ruts a way. They go over a low rise and out of Maplegate’s land.

You stand on the rise a long time. You do not know what any of it means. You do not know whether these eleven trees were a lawful thinning; you do not know how the boundary is to be reckoned after that stream changed course; you do not know whether ruts like these count as evidence in forestry at all.

You are a man who keeps accounts.

You are about to turn back when you hear somebody calling below.

One call, a pause, another. That is how position is confirmed in woodland.

A man comes up from the foot of the slope. Thirties, dark green coat, a canvas bag over his shoulder.
variants.unmet:
Seeing you, he stops short and then laughs.

“The new steward at Maplegate?” He puts out his hand. “Thierry Vallant. Forester, north district.”

There is bark grit on his hand; he wipes it on his trousers first.

“Are you up here about these stumps as well?” he asks, in passing.
variants.met:
“Steward.” He is not surprised in the least. “I did say I am in this wood two hundred days of the year.”

He walks to the nearest stump. He does not look at you first. He looks at the tree.

“This one is new.”

“What do you make of it?”

choices.text: This is Millridge cutting over the line

effects.logEntry: You declared to the forester’s face that this was Millridge cutting over the line.

choices.resultText:
He says “mm”, crouches at the nearest stump and scrapes the cut face with a finger.

“Over the line depends on the boundary, and the boundary depends on that stream,” he says. “The stream changed course last year. Which year’s course you reckon by after a change, I do not know either. You would want the survey file, and the file is at the chancery.”

He stands up.

“If you have your conclusion already then I will say no more about it.”

He pats the canvas bag and starts down the slope. A few steps on he turns round.

“One thing, though. Do not say it that certainly in front of other people. You have no evidence yet.”

choices.text: This is an internal estate matter. I shall report to the duchy once the survey is settled

effects.logEntry: You said it was an internal estate matter and that you would report to the duchy in due course.

choices.resultText:
He stops short.

“Report to the duchy.” He repeats it.

Then he laughs, and it is not the same laugh he had when he first saw you.

“Right. You report, then.” He shoulders the canvas bag again. “I am the duchy.”

He goes two steps down the slope and stops, and his tone comes back to easy.

“I am not trying to score off you. Two weeks in the post, of course you do not know the procedure,” he says. “But next time you run into me in the woods, you can just ask. I am in here two hundred days of the year.”

He goes.

choices.text: Honestly, I cannot read it. Whether this is over the line, I cannot say

effects.logEntry: You told the forester you could not judge whether it was over the line.

choices.resultText:
He whistles.

“That is very good news,” he says. “The last steward who told me he could read a wood had me correcting his felling declarations for three months.”

He crouches, takes a small rule out of the canvas bag, measures the diameter of three cut faces and counts the rings. He measures fast, and he measures every one of them twice.

“These are between thirty-two and thirty-eight at breast height,” he says. “Thirty-eight is the interesting number. Across every lawful felling declaration in the north district this year, the diameter limit is thirty.”

He stands and brushes off his hands.

“Anything over thirty wants separate approval, because an oak that size on this slope takes about sixty years. Four of these eleven are over.”

You ask him what that means.

“It means somebody declared one thing and cut another,” he says. He says it lightly, with nothing serious in it at all. “Or somebody measured wrong. People measure wrong.”

He glances at the skid road running north.

“But a skid road does not run the wrong way.”
